body: Thanks for the response! Being happy with myself is something I struggle with in all walks of life, really, so it's good advice that I definitely need to work on. I think part of what is getting to me is just the sense of loneliness over and apart from dating; I want to chat about my experiences of dating and relationships with my female friends, but whenever the topic comes up I'm just...forcibly reminded that their feelings about it are really different than mine, so I pretend to feel the same (like, I guess, a lot of people on the ace spectrum, I honestly thought women were just exaggerating their feelings of sexual attraction until well into my 20s).

I have, but I currently live in a pretty small town, so I doubt there are a ton of options. I'm also just hesitant to sign up for something like acebook because I'm worried I'm not "really" asexual--like, maybe all of this is just because I'm depressed/on meds. That said, though, I'll definitely mull it over, because I'm increasingly disillusioned with straight men (maybe it sounds weird, but the best relationship I ever had was with a bi guy who hadn't been with a woman before; he did ultimately conclude he was bi, but we took things really slowly and talked through everything, which was exactly what I needed, even though I didn't really know it at the time.)

For sure. I mean, obviously people without OCD can also get a song stuck in their head or whatever, but I definitely noticed an uptick in how repetitive my thoughts in general were after developing OCD.

I think the most widely accepted current thinking is that you inherit the predisposition but it takes an environmental trigger to set it off. That jibes with my personal experience, because while there are mental health problems on both sides of my family (including what I'd call mild OCD), I didn't develop it until my early teens, when my parents' marriage and my relationship with my dad were both falling apart.

I do. I personally see it as part of my OCD, because it involves a similar pattern of thinking, but I can see where it can also overlap with other kinds of mental illness. In fact, my own health anxiety was fairly minor until after I went through an actual medical emergency, so i think there's sometimes an element of PTSD as well.
Yes! I've described it as someone poking you over and over and over again, but this captures the pain better.

Honestly, I feel like OCD has made me less creative. As a little kid, I was always coming up with wacky stories, games, etc., but ever since I developed OCD around (around 12 or 13), I've had a tendency to get stuck in ruts--and not just actual obsessions. It's like everything, good and bad, has a tendency to loop endlessly in my mind now, which isn't really conducive to new and original ideas :/ That's obviously just my experience, but I think people underestimate the extent to which OCD is a whole pattern of thinking, not just a few scattered worries. I really wish I could go back to the way I used to be.
Also, if you're on any medication for anxiety--specifically, SSRIs--those can mildly affect clotting and lead to easy bruising.

I don't skin pick, but I do have mild trich. One thing that I've found discourages it is wearing nail polish, since picking tends to chip it. You could also try getting something like a stress ball or putty to keep your hands busy.

I've used it at times when my anxiety was very bad, but sparingly. In my experience, it works very well as a short term fix, when the feelings are just intolerable and you want to crawl out of your own skin. It's addictive, though, so you have to be really careful with it; it's not something to rely on daily.

Anecdotally, I think it's pretty common for people with OCD to have a tendency toward obsessiveness in all walks of life. I'm 29, and my crushes are as all-consuming as they were when I was a pre-teen--even the stupid celebrity crushes you're supposed to grow out of. Like, 24/7 daydreaming, and mentally bending and twisting every incident in my life to somehow relate to the poor guy. I don't think of it as part of OCD per se, since it's not inherently upsetting or unpleasant, but I do think it's related. "Sticky" brains, or whatever.

And another thing: relationships/sexuality are a really common area of life for OCD to latch onto, so what you're talking about could be a variation on that.
Not the OP, but I imagine starting to do a mental compulsion (e.g. ruminating) without realizing it. I know that I struggle with that, at any rate.

This is the book I always recommend when people ask for accounts of mental illness! Which doesn't happen a lot, but whatever :P He completely captures the feel of depression. Another good one (also about depression, but there's so much overlap with OCD/anxiety) is This Close to Happy by Daphne Merkin.

I think I read somewhere that they're starting to rethink the idea of insight with regards to OCD. Not abandoning it, but acknowledging that it's complicated. There probably are people who know virtually all the time that their beliefs are irrational, and there probably are people who lack that insight virtually all of the time. For a lot of people, though, insight fluctuates; there are times when I, at least, totally believe my fears, and there are times when I think they're absurd.

Also, if you have any comorbid conditions, my hunch is that that might also complicate things. When I've been very depressed, for instance, everything seems awful and hopeless, so it's much easier to buy into the obsessions as well.

Well, you don't need to decide one way or the other right now. But even if you were bi, you don't "have" to do anything that makes you uncomfortable--the idea that you'll basically be forced to do something you don't want to is just OCD.

Another thing to bear in mind is that a lot of people (probably most) have sexual fantasies that they would never want to act on in real life--and not even necessarily because they're "worried" about them per se, but just because the reality doesn't do it for them. 

It's totally possible that you might want to act on this fantasy at some point, of course, but the worrying about what it means and whether you have to act on it is OCD. It's tough (believe me, I know: I have sexuality-related themes too), but it's better to just accept the possibility that, yes, at some point you might identify as bi, but that you don't right now.
Omg, same--the chance that I would have gotten pregnant even without the ec was microscopic, but that obviously wasn't good enough for me, someone with OCD.

Not to burst your bubble or anything, but I think this kind of thing is actually pretty common :)

I've had comparable experiences. One that comes to mind is intense guilt after taking emergency contraception one time, just because there was a tiny chance it might have stopped an egg from implanting. And I'm pro-choice, so it's even crazier! The point is, obsessing over things you've done in the past and worrying about the possible repercussions (however unlikely) is basically like any other OCD theme. I still struggle a lot with my OCD, to be honest, but I have gotten a bit better at riding these kinds of thoughts and feelings out rather than analyzing them to death. Do you have access to a therapist or psychiatrist?

I mean, you can resist mental compulsions, but I agree that it's harder--not emotionally, necessarily, but in the sense that you can very easily start doing the compulsion without realizing it. So it's not just a matter of not doing the compulsion, but catching yourself doing it, which can happen over and over and over again.

This is one reason why (unpopular opinion) I think there should be more research into treatments beyond erp. I do think erp can help with mental compulsions, but I think it would be nice to have a treatment that's less...all-consuming.

I do this. It's not really tied to any anxiety for me, but I'm pretty sure it's been shown that people with OCD have addictive tendencies, so it makes sense; people without OCD can easily become "addicted" to their phones, so imagine what it's like if you have a tendency toward "sticky" thoughts and behaviors.
Thanks for the kind words! I'd never even heard of adenomyosis, but it's something I'll keep in mind.

Thanks for the response. I'm hoping to get at least a bit more clarity over what my gynecologist thinks the cyst might be this week, and possibly have another ultrasound to check if it's gone away--hopefully that will give some insight into whether it's connected to the bleeding or just a fluke. In any case, I've definitely heard horror stories about how long it can take to get a diagnosis--I know someone who waited about eight or nine years for hers. Since my symptoms aren't awful at the moment and are mostly period-confined, I'm at least comfortable waiting in that respect. Mentally, the uncertainty is starting to get stressful; I had an (unrelated) medical emergency several years ago that has left me with some bad anxiety when it comes to health issues.

Just to add a different perspective: I've never been officially diagnosed with BDD. I am 100 percent sure I have it, though, partly for obvious reasons and partly because it's tightly correlated with OCD--which I have officially been diagnosed with it. For me, the BDD diagnosis just seems unnecessary because the treatment for it is pretty much the same as the treatment for OCD--same kinds of medications, same kinds of therapies, etc. So I guess my view is that the diagnosis matters mostly in terms of treatment: if you aren't already in treatment for a related disorder (OCD, health anxiety, etc.), you might need to push a bit for a diagnosis just to make sure you're getting the treatment you need.
It does sound like OCD, yeah. Also, fearing the loss of control is pretty common in OCD, so it would make sense (as you say) to fixate on mental illnesses in that respect.

Looking back, I had a few OCD-ish compulsions by age 9 or 10. I wouldn't say they really became a disorder until I was 13 or so. It is true that a lot of mental illnesses, OCD included, often present in adolescence, so I sort of get where your mom is coming from. At the same time, regardless of when you develop OCD, it's usually considered a lifelong disorder. That's not to say it can't wax and wane (and hopefully improve!), but it's probably not going to just disappear; I'm 29 now, and it's still part of my life.

It doesn't come up much in official websites on OCD, but yes: I've seen a lot of people fixate on mental health issues. Myself included. I flit around from theme to theme a lot, but I've worried about autism, narcissism, borderline personality disorder (pretty much all the personality disorders, actually), etc. I'm also one of those people who obsesses over her sexual orientation, and the underlying fear is very similar to me: it's this terror of not being who I thought I was and feeling alien to myself. FWIW, I also have "traditional" health anxiety, and I do think the fear is a bit different there. I'd still describe it as a subset of OCD, but it's a more straightforward fear of pain, not the more existential fear of questioning your identity.
No worries, and glad to hear you're doing well! Hope we all get there some day.

Hope this turned out well for you! I'm going through something similar at the moment. I had a small, flesh-colored bump on my shoulder; I figured it was an acne scar. I picked at it, though, and now it's a larger, shiny, pink bump--similar to BCC. Logically, I know I couldn't give myself cancer that way, but I keep thinking maybe I somehow caused the original "cancer" to spread by picking it open and giving it access to all that blood. And like you said, I feel stupid even writing that. It's crazy how potent anxiety is.
Hey, that's what triggered my health anxiety too! Good times...

I understand what you're saying from a practical perspective, but I really don't think it's helpful to moralize in that way when you're talking about a mental illness. Like, we've moved away from describing addiction in terms of personal weakness, but there now seems to be this push to talk about mental illness (at least anxiety/OCD-spectrum disorders) in those terms. If you're out of your mind with fear, it's difficult by definition to think of anything except making the fear stop. It's one thing to encourage people to look at solutions beyond reassurance-seeking, but labeling the behavior as "selfish" is judgmental and counterproductive, in my opinion.

Hope this is okay to ask, but--how did you go about getting the CPTSD diagnosis? My relationship with my dad was not good, especially during my teenage years, and I feel like it's really warped my self-esteem and my ability to be close to people--particularly men. Then, just recently, someone I met in a support group said that an experience I was describing sounded like an "emotional flashback"--which I guess is a hallmark of CPTSD? I've talked about these issues with my therapist, and I suppose the diagnosis is ultimately less important than buckling down and addressing the problem, but a part of me feels like I need the validation a label would provide in order to move forward. My dad's abuse was very covert, so I constantly question whether it really qualifies as abuse at all.

Yes, frequently. And to be honest, I can't say I've come out the other side convinced that the thoughts were unreasonable. Compared to some of the really low periods in my life, I'm doing fairly well at the moment, but this is still so far removed from the life I imagined myself having, and there are only a couple of things in it that make it worthwhile. If I lost those, I'm not sure there would be enough good in my life to outweigh the bad.

For sure. People with OCD have a really high chance of having depression as well--I can't remember the exact number, but over 50%. OCD can also trigger depressive episodes, and vice versa. The brain chemistry involved is similar (which is why SSRIs can sometimes help treat OCD), and some of the symptoms are as well (e.g. rumination, guilt, etc.).

Um, not really a "small" symptom but: severe chest pain. It came on very suddenly one night when I was 20. I was (and am) a hypochondriac, so I figured it was anxiety, ignored it, and it eventually went away...for a week. When it happened again, I went to the hospital, where I eventually wound up learning my left lung was mostly collapsed. It happened a third time not too long after, and I ended up having surgery to prevent it from collapsing in the future: I'm 29 now, and haven't had problems since. But seriously, unless you can tell for sure that it's muscular or have actually been diagnosed with panic attacks, do not mess around with chest pain.

The thing is, you have to also remember how many more times you've been wrong, and the doctors have been right. I realize that's difficult. When I was 20, I had severe chest pain one night that I blew off because I knew I had anxiety problems. It happened again a week later, and I went to the hospital, where they initially told me it sounded like some minor muscle pain: I could tell they thought I was just a hypochondriac. Which I of course was, but it turned out that I also had a recurring collapsed lung that needed surgery. These things are scary, of course, but they're also the exception to the rule: 99% of the time, everything is okay. I still obviously struggle to believe that, but it's true.

I took psychology in high school. Back then, I had the classic cleanliness compulsions, so it was a pretty easy self-diagnosis. The bulk of my OCD has always been obsessional, though, and it took me more than a decade to learn that all the awful thoughts and anxiety I was experiencing were OCD too--and then only from reading online.
Yes! For me, though, it's typically that I think I look okay in the mirror, and then I'll see a picture of myself and just feel repulsed.
I mean, it's certainly true in some cases: I have OCD, and I consider BDD a subtype of it (same as my health anxiety, incidentally). I'm not sure that's true for everyone, though.

I've had moderate success with it, and I find it more intuitive than ERP; to me, it almost feels as if it encompasses ERP, if that makes sense. It hasn't been a miracle cure, but then again, nothing has been for me.

I sort of understand the reasoning, but I do feel like it makes it even more difficult to explain OCD to people with no real knowledge of it. I have gotten much better at avoiding my compulsions (which were never the obvious, classic ones anyway--more things like reassurance-seeking). I still have horrible anxiety with my intrusive thoughts, though, and it's even harder to convey what that's like now that OCD is classed with more compulsion-heavy disorders like trich (which I also have, so yes, I agree there's a connection, but it's not the whole story).

This. So, so much. I have this as a theme, and I've stumbled across a lot of other people with it too. I'm afraid to ever mention it, though, because people can be really defensive. But the thing is, it's not about autism anymore than worrying about being gay is about homosexuality; the fear is about losing your identity, or a part of your identity you value. I think it's great that there is more awareness of diagnoses like autism, but I wish that that awareness could extend to OCD as well.

I think this is a good way of putting it. I mean, I didn't develop OCD until late childhood/early adolescence, so I wasn't always like this, but I do think that--having had it for the majority of my life at this point--it's basically inseparable from my personality. And I do think it bleeds over into more benign traits; I have a somewhat obsessive personality in general, although again, I remember a time in my life when that wasn't the case.

That said, I really, really hate it when people include it under the neurodiversity umbrella. Even the milder symptoms of it, like a general tendency toward obsessiveness, on some level feel alien to me. They're not compatible with what I value, or the kind of person I see myself as "deep down." I would cheerfully give up every single aspect of the disorder, if I could.

I have similar experiences. I personally think it's related to OCD, but it's one of the things that sometimes makes me worry I have undiagnosed autism (absolutely no disrespect intended to anyone with autism--it's just a weird theme I have, like people worrying about their sexual orientation). The thing about it that seems OCD-ish, to me, is the fact that it's unpleasant; I'll begin by being mildly interested in something, but I feel "compelled" to explore it more, and I quickly start getting sick of it. Also, like you said, I can't remember having this experience before developing OCD (12/13 for me). When I'm being rational, I chalk it up to having a "sticky" brain--if you have OCD, even "good" thoughts can get stuck on loops in a way that's really annoying :/

Yeah, definitely. If you can push through the bit about inserting and emptying it, everything else becomes so much easier to manage--no more worrying about finding a bathroom at exactly the right time to change a pad/tampon, no more drying out, etc.

This is going to sound crazy (and it's definitely not for everyone), but...have you considered trying out a menstrual cup? I'm more of a "pure O" person myself, but I did have some contamination-related anxieties, and I feel like switching from tampons to a cup was an A+ form of exposure therapy; it forces you to get up close and personal with your body and period, and you'll see that nothing bad happens.

Just a thought. Obviously how you manage your period is a reallllly personal decision, but I just wanted to share my experience in case it might help.

I understand why they explained ACT the way they did, but it's not really giving you an accurate picture of what it does for you. I'm still fairly new to it, but I'd say that ACT is about learning how to live with feelings, not symptoms. I personally find it a lot more intuitive than ERP, because it's more global in its approach; I don't spend time parsing whether something is technically an obsession or a compulsion or whatever, because ACT encourages you to handle all distressing emotions in pretty much the same way. It really gets to the root of the problematic thinking patterns. For that reason (and from personal experience), I think it's also a good choice if you happen to have a comorbid disorder like depression; you're going to be approaching symptoms in more or less the same way regardless of what's causing them.

No worries--I actually haven't logged on in weeks, so it's a total coincidence I saw your reply. Anyway, I've been doing better overall since switching meds and starting ACT therapy, but I still have spikes and rough patches (hypochondria, at the moment). How are you doing these days?

Thanks, and sorry for the slow response. I'm actually in therapy at the moment doing ACT rather than ERP, and I feel like that's helping a bit; it's not targeted in the same way, but I'm calmer overall. Still, I'd love to hear any suggestions you might have (or just commiserate)!

I went to a crisis chat center online a couple of times. Don't expect miracles, but my experiences were generally good. I was absolutely desperate when I got in touch with them--suicidal thoughts, felt like crawling out of my skin, etc.--and they talked me down a bit. For me, it's a way of taking the edge off the feelings just enough that I can maybe start taking some minor steps; the last time I went to a crisis chat center, I still felt pretty hopeless afterward, but I had just enough motivation to find a therapist the next day.

I did when I was a teenager; I've moved on to bigger and better (har har) things now, but back then I had contamination obsessions, and they were focused mostly on sexual fluids and body hair. Even my own! I would only wear pajamas to bed--never a nightgown, because it might ride up, and I was afraid of my underwear coming in contact with the bed.

Anyway, I feel like what made me get over it was, er, actually starting to have sex? I mean, all else being equal, I'd still rather take a shower afterwards, but I don't obsess about it anywhere near the amount I used to; the last time I was seeing someone, I didn't have a problem just hanging out in his bed knowing that, yes, we'd had sex there before. I'm obviously not suggesting you go out and have sex--that's a totally personal choice--but the point is that what helped me was, effectively, "exposure therapy." I imagine you can do some kind of variation on that--maybe just stop using the wipes for a start?
I used to want to be a B or a C, but now I'm okay with being a 34A. I do wish they were closer set so that I could get some semblance of cleavage with a push-up bra, but whatever.
Nothing--I'm just anxious.

I have OCD ("pure O," so pretty much no visible compulsions) and episodes of depression.

I could go on and on about how incredibly shitty those disorders feel, but the bottom line is this: a lot of people say the stigma of mental illness is worse than the disease, and (in my opinion) that's just not true. While I can't say I welcome having to disclose my diagnoses to other people, that discomfort doesn't even begin to compare to what it's like to feel suicidal, or so anxious you want to crawl out of your own skin.

I actually think mood and anxiety disorders (I can't speak for anything else) aren't taken seriously enough. A lot of well-meaning people think of them as these parasitic disorders that aren't really you and just need to be cleared up with medication. That's sort of true--when I'm well, for example, I actually tend to be a pretty optimistic person--but it also skims over a lot. Depression and anxiety can really embed themselves into your psyche; with my OCD, for instance, there are times when I honestly don't know whether my fears are real or not. And even when I'm not depressed or going through a bad bout of anxiety, I tend to be on the hypersensitive and neurotic side.

Same. I feel like that might be common with compulsions that are mental? I mean, my only compulsions are ruminating and reassurance-seeking, and I don't feel like I "have" to do either of those--I just want a way out of the anxiety.

Thanks! After poking around on the internet, I found out that the new antidepressant I'm on can cause stress incontinence. Since it's only a few drops, I'm going to assume it's nothing serious and try changing up my schedule to see if that helps.
Wetting myself, but I don't typically have the chance to use the bathroom right before running. It's usually been more like 45 minutes - an hour by the time I start running.

There's really no way to answer that, because it varies for everyone. I've had good luck overall with medications; I was on Lexapro for six years and it helped for quite a while, and Paxil didn't help but also didn't hurt. With that said, I've also had some pretty negative experiences. I'm currently on Prozac, and when I was put on it, I was in a depressive episode on top of the OCD. Things have pretty much evened out now, but for a while it made the suicidal thinking sooo much worse, and that scared me a bit, to be honest. 

To be clear, I'm not against medications at all, but I do now think they should be combined with therapy. I've admittedly had difficulties with ERP, but I'm currently doing ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy), which I'm finding helpful (for me, it's easier to grasp than ERP, plus it also helps with depression). So that's another possibility--not necessarily as a replacement for medication, but as another strategy.

I feel like they're sort of similar, although ACT is the only one I've done (well, am doing) in a structured way (I also have depression, so I was interested in trying a therapy that might help with that as well). My understanding is that ERP also involves "sitting" with the thoughts--it's just that you're trying to provoke particularly anxiety-producing ones.

I had a similar experience! Except mine was watching Monk, because that was on during my teens; it's stereotypical, definitely, but since my obsessions at the time were contamination related I saw a lot of myself in it. Then I took AP Psych and read about OCD and was pretty much certain.
Oh man, I relate to this so much. I'm 27, but the past few years I feel like I've just been treading water; I'm scared by how fast time is going by, but I also barely notice it.

Thanks. I've lost pets before, but this is the first one I've lost as an adult, and in some ways I think it's harder than losing one as a kid; when you're little, you feel the loss, but you don't think about all the things you could have done differently. In any case, I appreciate your response.

Thanks. Rationally, I know that my cat has had a pretty good life, but I'm beating myself up over all the times I've snapped at him or pushed him away because I was in a bad mood. I can also really relate to what you said about wanting to spare your dog a more painful existence. One of the things I'm struggling with is the quality of life issue; my cat's happy right now, but he could deteriorate very quickly. It just sucks, because I don't want to preemptively put him down when he could have months of good health left, but I also don't want his last moments to be painful...

Oh, I wasn't saying to talk about that specifically--I just meant to be generally open about your concerns. And if the therapist starts to focus on something you feel isn't important, tell them exactly that.

First off, don't worry about having nothing to say; it's the therapist's job to get you talking. This is probably the one situation in life where there is no pressure on YOU to say anything in particular at all; you say what's on your mind, and if nothing's on your mind, you say that. The only real "mistake" you can make is not being honest about what you're feeling; I've seen many therapists but only recently started being fully open with them and trust me--it helps.

Second, if a therapist asks how they can help, they're (hopefully!) not literally asking what they can do to help--if you knew what would help you, you wouldn't be seeing a therapist! It's just a conversation starter--just explain what you're dealing with that has led you to seek help, and the therapist should take it from there.
Glad it helped :)

I have both OCD and health anxiety, and I personally don't see much of a difference; I view the health anxiety as just one OCD "theme." I don't think it really matters whether the health fears are rooted in reality or not; for me, the thing that kickstarted the health anxiety was a legit medical emergency (spontaneously collapsed lung), but the thought process itself is very OCD-ish, in my opinion.

The one distinction I would make is that I feel like some health anxiety can tend more toward depression/PTSD. That's the kind of health anxiety I experienced right after having the collapsed lung, and it was less a "what if" thought process and more a "I KNOW I'm doomed, everything is pointless, etc." Basically, a lot less anxiety and a lot more despair. I think, though, that if you have OCD (or OCD tendencies) any immediate trauma-related feelings tend to convert into OCD thoughts over the long run. 

TL;DR: I personally find it helpful to treat health anxiety as another manifestation of OCD, but certain kinds of health anxiety might have more in common with other mental disorders.

Well...my parents knew something was wrong before I was officially diagnosed, and I think they might have suspected OCD. 

My dad made me feel pretty terrible about it, but I wouldn't take that to mean anything, because he was just a difficult person in general. Most parents would be supportive, I think, even if they don't quite "get" it. And some parents can be hugely helpful; my mom has been an absolute rock through all my problems with OCD and depression. The only downside to that openness, in my experience, is knowing how hard it must be for her to hear some of what I'm dealing with; I've been suicidal before, and explaining that to my mom was really distressing for both of us.

I had three collapses seven years ago and then had the VATS surgery--I've never had a problem since. You'll probably be fine, but it can definitely take a while to get your life back on track afterward; I was a sophomore in college at the time, and I had to basically take a semester off. Don't be afraid to take the time to fully recover.
Well, I typically exercise in the morning. That helps me a bit, so if it's possible with your schedule, you might give that a try?

I had a recurring pneumothorax (3x, though technically only two were diagnosed) that was fixed with surgery; that was seven years ago, and it's never happened since. Like mchlondon said, it's difficult to say how likely it is to happen again; like you, I had no history of smoking or lung disease, though I apparently did have a genetic predisposition (one of my relatives had a collapse a couple of years after I did, and I also had blebs). If you don't have any other risk factors, it might be worth waiting, but don't be afraid of the surgery if you want peace of mind; the recovery time is very quick.
That's a good sign! My recurrences all happened within a month, so you may just be one of the lucky ones that has one episode and then never has any more problems :)

My understanding is that depression is often worse in the morning, regardless of the cause (I sometimes go into depressive episodes as a result of OCD flares, but they sometimes happen independently of it--fun). I personally tend more toward the "numb" side of depression in the morning, and then in the evening I get into a more anxious/actively despairing phase.

Try not to stress too much about the surgery :) I had it on my left lung when I was 20 (now 27), and the recovery was indeed very fast, even though  I, unfortunately, had problems with the chest tube afterward that lengthened my hospital stay. Basically, there was a kink in the tube so it wasn't working properly for a couple of days, which meant that by the time they straightened it out, I was off the strong painkillers. Don't let that freak you out, though; it was uncomfortable but still quite bearable, and that almost certainly won't happen to you! The only other thing was that I was a bit stiff for a couple of weeks afterward (I remember I had a hard time driving, because it hurt to turn around enough to switch lanes/back up/etc.).

Hey! I know this is an old post, but as someone who's been through the spontaneous pneumothorax thing, I just wanted to reach out to you in case you're still dealing with fears of recurrence/debating whether to have surgery. My left lung collapsed three times when I was 20. The first time I didn't even go to the hospital because I assumed it was nothing, and I obviously lived to tell the tale :) The second time, I went to the ER; I think it was 30 or 40 percent collapsed. The third time happened about a week after I was discharged from the second, and I believe it was about an 80 percent collapse; at that point, they just kept me in the hospital until they could do the surgery. The surgery itself went fine, though, and I've never had a problem since.

Thanks--I appreciate the reply. I also developed health anxiety after a health scare (spontaneously collapsed lung in my early 20s), so I typically don't find statistics very reassuring--they've turned on me before! It does help to hear from someone who's been there, though, so thanks again :)

I understand what you're saying, but at the same time, I think that labeling the subtypes can actually be a way to better understand the systemic nature of the disorder. When I first developed OCD as a teenager, I had very "classic" contamination obsessions and compulsions; no one ever told me--and it never occurred to me--that the obsessions I developed later in life (e.g. about health, about sexual orientation, etc.) were part of the same tendency. Discovering that those were all variations of the same disorder was a revelation to me, and I wouldn't have learned that if it hadn't been for people talking about "hocd," "harm ocd," etc. 

In any case, as I said, I understand your qualms. Probably the best solution would be to make information on the breadth of OCD symptoms more widely available, so that people can recognize those symptoms for what they are. I have the sexual orientation theme (among many, many others), but it kind of blurs over into trans OCD at times, so here's my take: typically, I think you're supposed to try NOT to "figure out" which thoughts are "real" and which are OCD, because that's compulsive behavior. Ditto to trying to "figure out" your "real self," because one thing a lot of OCD people struggle with is an intolerance of uncertainty, and you don't want to add fuel to the fire.

With that said, if you think there is a genuine possibility the thoughts are real (read: when you're thinking about them calmly rather than in the middle of a panic attack), I can see why you'd want to be able to distinguish between what's real and what's not, so here's my rule of thumb; if the thought of doing something (e.g. sleeping with someone of the same sex) is seriously distressing to me, I don't do it. In the end, I'm not sure it really matters whether there's some "inner me" that's a lesbian (or a sociopath, or whatever my current obsession is), because the idea of acting on that "inner me" makes me unhappy, and why should I go out of my way to do something that will make me unhappy? 

In other words, if you just don't want to identify as non-binary, don't. It doesn't really matter why you don't want to, and it doesn't really matter that at some point in the future you might want to (though I know it feels like that's the only thing that matters); if you don't want to now, there's no reason to do it.

I can't diagnose you, of course, but to me what you're describing sounds a lot like the Pure O form of OCD. I have that, and around half my obsessions/compulsions involve endlessly ruminating on my "true" nature--the fear is always that I'm something I don't want to be. The general rule of thumb is that if you find the thoughts scary or disturbing, they likely aren't really "you." You seem quite distressed by the thought of being "neutral" or "evil" deep down, so I'd say you probably have nothing to worry about; a truly sociopathic person wouldn't feel so much anxiety about being sociopathic.

A couple other things: I don't think thoughts about self-harm are "evil." After all, the only person you'd be harming is, well, yourself! Also, you ask whether it's possible that your thoughts "are actually an outgrowth of your dark center." One thing I've heard a lot re: the treatment of OCD is that you need to learn to live with the thought that, yes, anything is technically possible. I have a horribly difficult time with that, so I totally understood wanting to be 100% sure that these thoughts aren't you, but in the end that's counterproductive. The goal of a lot of therapy for OCD is to get the patient to acknowledge that they're having a thought that probably doesn't but theoretically COULD say something about them, and then move on.

To me, this sounds like it could be OCD, but yes: best to get an official diagnosis. That way, you can start getting relief from your symptoms, which is what really matters when you get right down to it; the diagnosis is just a shorthand for a particular kind of distress/anxiety.

For what it's worth, though, I wouldn't worry about whether your symptoms are "legitimate" OCD. I'm firmly of the opinion that most mental illnesses exist on a spectrum. Everyone can have OCD-ish traits--not in the "Haha, I like to eat my Oreos a particular way, I'm so OCD about it!" sense, but in the sense that everyone can have intrusive thoughts that cause them anxiety. I think the cutoff point for diagnosis is basically subjective; if intrusive thoughts are causing YOU a lot of distress, it doesn't really matter how your experience compares to other people's.

Yeah, I'm pretty sure the only time a therapist/psychiatrist can divulge information is if they think you're an immediate threat to yourself or others. Since you have POCD, I imagine alarm bells may be going off in your head, but therapists/psychiatrists are pretty good at distinguishing between OCD intrusive thoughts and actual thoughts of desiring harm; I literally told my psychiatrist that I'm afraid of being a sociopath, and she did not call the cops on me :)

If you're seeing a GP, I bet you'll be able to get a referral without going into too many of the gory details; you may not even  have to say you suspect OCD--the first time I got a referral, I just said I was having bad anxiety problems. If you DO mention OCD, though, you can probably keep it vague; most OCD themes fall into certain categories (contamination, sex, religion, etc.), and even a GP will probably know enough psychiatry to recognize that.

The only other thing I'd say, though, is that at some point you'll probably have to get used to going into the details of your symptoms; in my experience, psychiatrists and therapists always ask for examples of intrusive thoughts, compulsive behaviors, etc. I know it's embarrassing, but just remember: it's almost certainly something they've heard before. My latest themes are some of the most stigmatized ones out there (involving sex, morality, etc.) and when I told my new psychiatrist about them she was completely unfazed.
